A.text: Count how many separate groups of towns exist by joining towns that share a road. While processing each road, merge the two groups that contain its endpoints. After all roads are handled, the remaining number of groups is the island count, and the size of the biggest group gives the largest island. This merging structure lets you update group sizes efficiently.

d3.evidence: The hint describes the high-level approach using connected components and union-find concepts without detailing code structure or exact implementation logic.

A.text: Count how many separate groups of towns exist by joining towns that share a road. While joining, keep track of how many towns are in each group. After processing all roads, the total number of groups gives the island count, and the biggest recorded group size is the answer for the largest island. This works because any towns that can reach each other will end up in the same group.

d3.evidence: The hint describes the high-level approach using plain words without giving code, exact algorithms, or low-level implementation details.

A.text: Your loop starts a fresh flood‑fill from every town and never remembers which towns were already visited, so you repeat the same traversals many times. Switch to a single traversal per component (for example, keep a global visited array or use a union‑find structure) so each town is processed only once; that will reduce the complexity to linear and eliminate the timeout.
